p189.lead: The morontia resurrection at Joseph’s tomb at two minutes past three on Sunday morning, the true reason the tomb was empty, and the first call: “Mary.”

p189.foot.text: Narrated by a secondary midwayer once assigned to the Apostle Andrew

p189.s0.h: Introduction — What No Creature Could Do
p189.s0.b0: Shortly after Jesus was buried, the chief of the archangels then on Urantia convened a council of resurrection on his own initiative to consider how Jesus might be restored. It was not Gabriel who called them; Michael’s creatures came together on their own responsibility. By about midnight they had concluded that there was nothing creatures could do to assist their Creator’s resurrection.
p189.s0.b1: Gabriel reminded them that Michael had laid down his life of his own free will and therefore had the power to take it up again. Then Jesus’ Personalized Adjuster, who was directing the celestial hosts, explained to those waiting what was now taking place.
p189.s0.b3: The Adjuster told them that their Creator-father had chosen to pass through the whole experience of his mortal creatures — from birth on a material world, through natural death and morontia resurrection, into true spirit existence. From Gabriel down to the humblest cherubim, all waited patiently without understanding.
p189.s1.h: I. The Morontia Transit — Stone and Seal Undisturbed
p189.s1.b0: At a quarter to three on Sunday morning, the incarnation commission of seven Paradise personalities took its place around the tomb. At ten minutes before three, intense vibrations of combined material and morontia activities began to issue from the tomb, and at two minutes past three on April 9, A.D. 30, the resurrected morontia form and personality of Jesus came forth from the tomb.
p189.s1.b1: Yet the body of flesh in which he had lived for almost thirty-six years still lay in the niche, wrapped in linen. The stone had not been moved, Pilate’s seal was unbroken, and the guards noticed nothing. At this point the narrator raises the question of how matter, morontia, and spirit are related.

head: Clear statements about the resurrection
What they say
rows: The material body was not part of the resurrected personality; it remained in the tomb
2. Not as spirit or as Michael

p189.s1.b4: The text says that no creature of this universe and no personality of any other universe had any part in this resurrection. The seven Paradise personalities surrounded the tomb but did nothing. He accomplished it all by a power that lay within himself.
p189.s1.b6: The risen Jesus first told Gabriel to continue in charge of universe affairs, had his brotherly greetings conveyed to Immanuel, and asked for the certification of the Ancients of Days. Then he spoke the first words of his postmortal career to the morontia groups of the seven mansion worlds who had gathered to welcome him.
p189.s1.b8: Jesus then began his induction into morontia life, a process that took more than an hour of earth time and was twice interrupted by his wish to communicate with his former associates in the flesh who came to look into the empty tomb. That the sovereign of a universe, in the very first hour of his new career, turned first to his grieving friends shows how personal his love is.
p189.s2.h: II. The Material Body of Jesus — Why the Tomb Was Empty
p189.s2.b0: At ten minutes past three, the chief of archangels asked Gabriel for custody of Jesus’ mortal remains. The celestial hosts did not want to remember the slow decay of the human form of their universe’s Creator. When permission was given, they took charge of the body with the help of the midwayers, since a material body could not pass out of the sealed tomb as the morontia form had done.
p189.s2.b1: When the secondary midwayers rolled away the huge, millstone-like stone, the guards saw it move apparently of its own accord and fled in terror. The leaders, on hearing their report, did not punish the guards; instead they paid each of the twenty to say that the disciples had taken the body away in the night.

head: Point
What the text explains
rows: Not because the body was restored or raised, but because the celestial hosts were permitted to dissolve it in a special way

Spiritual in nature, supported by the testimony of nearly a thousand people who met the risen Master

p189.s2.b4: Here the text offers a principle of thinking. Individual facts may be materially true, yet a conclusion drawn by joining them is not necessarily true spiritually. The truth of faith rests not on a combination of apparent facts but on living spiritual experience.
p189.s3.h: III. The Dispensational Resurrection — The Roll Call of the Sleeping
p189.s3.b0: About half past four in the morning, as Gabriel prepared for the general resurrection that would end the Adamic dispensation, the morontia Michael appeared and, declaring that the Father had given the Son to have life in himself, told him to begin the planetary roll call of resurrection. The circuit of the archangels operated from Urantia for the first time, and the survivors who had fallen asleep since the days of Adam appeared in the resurrection halls of mansonia.
p189.s3.b2: Ordinarily their seraphic guardians would have been present in mansonia when they awoke, but on this occasion they were still on this world, because Gabriel had to remain on Urantia in connection with Jesus’ resurrection. That the resurrection of one person coincided with the awakening of so many sleepers adds weight to this section.

head: Planetary roll call
When
rows: At the coming of the Planetary Prince
At the morontia resurrection, the mortal transit, of Jesus of Nazareth

p189.s3.b4: When the roll call began, the Personalized Adjuster relinquished command of the celestial hosts and departed for Salvington to register the completion of Michael’s mortal transit. Only Gabriel remained on Urantia with the morontia Jesus. The narrator explains that this account is written not from the limited human viewpoint but from that of those who actually saw these things.
p189.s4.h: IV. Discovery of the Empty Tomb — “Mary”
p189.s4.b0: Early that morning ten apostles were asleep in the upper room of Mark’s home. Thomas, unable to bear the sight of his fellows, had gone off to Bethpage to grieve alone. The text says the apostles’ distress arose less from doubt and despair than from fear, grief, and shame.
p189.s4.b1: A little before three, Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of the Alpheus twins, Salome, Joanna, and Susanna set out for the tomb with spices and bandages. They knew nothing of the guards or the seal. They were astonished to find the stone rolled away, and Mary Magdalene boldly went in and saw the empty niche and the grave cloths lying in order.
p189.s4.b2: As they went out through the Damascus gate, they paused when they met soldiers fleeing in terror toward the city, but then they hurried on. The faithfulness of these women, determined even in their grief to care for the Master’s body to the end, brought them to be the first to meet the risen Lord.
p189.s4.b3: At Mary’s scream the other women fled, but Joanna, ashamed to have deserted Mary, brought them back. They supposed the body had been moved, yet they could not explain the undisturbed grave cloths. Then a stranger appeared, and Mary took him to be the gardener.
p189.s4.b4: When he called her by name in his familiar voice, “Mary,” she knew him and fell to her knees. His appearance was so changed that she had not recognized him, but a single call of her name made him known. Human eyes could behold the morontia form only through the special ministry of the transformers and the midwayers.
p189.s4.b6: These words were not a rejection but guidance into a new relationship. Jesus was no longer a man of the flesh but a morontia being who would remain with them for a season before ascending to the Father. We can read them as a call to move beyond the wish to hold on to a loved one as he once was, and to accept a meeting on a higher level.
p189.s4.b7: Jesus told the women to go and tell his apostles — and Peter — that he had risen. At first the apostles thought it was a vision and would not believe, but when Peter heard that he had been named, he rushed out of the upper room, with John following.
p189.s5.h: V. Peter and John at the Tomb — Between Fear and Hope
p189.s5.b0: As Peter ran, his mind swung between fear and hope. He was afraid to meet the Master, but the news that a message had been sent especially to him revived his hope. Only then did the promise of the third day come back to his mind. In John’s soul there welled up an ecstasy of joy and hope.
p189.s5.b1: John, arriving first, looked in from the entrance, while Peter went straight inside. Peter thought the enemies had stolen the body, but John replied that if it had been stolen, the tomb would not have been left in such order. They went in again and examined the grave cloths closely.
p189.s5.b2: After they left, Mary, discouraged because no one would believe her, came back to the tomb, and as she wept the Master appeared to her again.
p189.s5.b4: When Mary told them again, the apostles still did not believe; but when Peter and John returned, they no longer mocked her and were filled with fear and apprehension. So the news of the resurrection began with the testimony of women.
p189.s6.b0: Paper 189 presents the resurrection not as a mysterious miracle story but as the Creator going first along the path every mortal will walk. Jesus came forth in the same morontia form as the ascenders of the mansion worlds. His resurrection is therefore the most concrete promise of our own survival after death.

p190.lead: Resurrection Sunday: David’s messengers carry the news first, while Jesus appears in turn to his family, to the women, to the Greeks, and to two brothers on the road to Emmaus.

p190.foot.text: Narrated by a secondary midwayer once assigned to the Apostle Andrew

p190.s0.h: Introduction — Jesus Living a Morontia Career
p190.s0.b0: The risen Jesus did not leave at once; he stayed for a while on Urantia. The text explains that this period corresponds to the morontia career that the mortals of Satania pass through on the mansion worlds. On the very world where he had lived as a mortal, he himself walked the next stage of the ascending mortal’s path.
p190.s0.b1: The text says that the bestowal of life which enabled him to rise from death is the same gift of eternal life that he gives to the believers of the kingdom. Jesus’ resurrection, then, does not end with him alone. Believers too will rise on the morning of the resurrection with the same type of transition body.

head: Feature of the morontia body
What the text says
rows: A transition body between the mortal body and spirit

Not a vision or hallucination; those who saw it really saw him
The form was hard to recognize, but his voice and personality were easily known

p190.s0.b4: The believers who saw Jesus after his resurrection were not deceived by visions; they truly saw him. The text says that this abiding faith in his resurrection was the central element that bound together all branches of the early gospel teaching. Teachers at Jerusalem and Alexandria, at Antioch and Philadelphia, differed on other points, yet were one in this faith.
p190.s0.b5: The text also notes the role of Mary Magdalene. As Peter was chief spokesman for the apostles, she was chief spokesman and leading teacher of the women’s corps. That this cautious woman boldly spoke to a stranger she took for the gardener shows how great her astonishment was before the empty tomb, and how deep her love.
p190.s1.h: I. Heralds of the Resurrection — David Zebedee’s Last Mission
p190.s1.b0: Because the apostles did not want Jesus to leave them, they had taken lightly his words about his death and resurrection. So they did not believe the women’s report; of the ten in the upper room, only John was disposed, however faintly, to believe. Most of them supposed the Jews had removed the body.
p190.s1.b1: The men received the women’s report in different ways. Most of those at the home of Nicodemus doubted, but Joseph of Arimathea and David, inclined to believe, hurried to examine the tomb and found everything as the women had said. They were the last to see the tomb in that condition, for at half past seven the captain of the temple guards, sent by the high priest, removed the grave cloths and threw them over the cliff.
p190.s1.b2: Having seen the tomb himself, David did not argue with the apostles. He simply stated his own belief, and as he left he dropped the bag of Judas into Matthew’s lap. Then he released the twenty-six messengers gathered at the home of Nicodemus from their oath and gave them one last assignment.
p190.s1.b5: The messengers did not wait to talk with those who had seen Jesus; they took David’s word and went. Even those who doubted somewhat carried the news with the same assurance and speed. They scattered to every center of believers, from Beersheba in the south to Sidon in the north, and from Philadelphia in the east to Alexandria in the west.

p190.s1.b8: It is worth noticing that the first proclamation of the resurrection came not from the apostles but from laymen. Office does not guarantee faith, and this scene shows that trust and courage may move first.
p190.s1.b9: After sending out his messengers, David took his mother and joined Jesus’ family at Bethany. He accompanied Martha and Mary as they disposed of their property and went to join Lazarus at Philadelphia, and he left Bethany the day after he married Ruth, Jesus’ youngest sister, in early June. Jesus’ mother Mary was taken by John Zebedee to his home at Bethsaida.
p190.s2.h: II. Jesus’ Appearance at Bethany — His Brother James and His Earthly Family
p190.s2.b0: From his resurrection to his ascension Jesus made nineteen separate appearances to believers. He did not appear to his enemies or to any who could not make spiritual use of the manifestation. The first and second appearances were to the women at the tomb and to Mary Magdalene; the third was to his eldest brother, James, at Bethany.
p190.s2.b1: James had wanted to believe in his brother’s mission, but he had long been estranged from the work and deeply doubted the claim to be the Messiah. As he stood by the empty tomb of Lazarus, he felt as if someone had touched him on the shoulder, and a strange form spoke his name.
p190.s2.b3: When James moved to kneel, Jesus bade him stand, and the two walked in the garden for almost three minutes, talking of the past and the future. That afternoon Jesus appeared to twenty family members and friends and asked why they had lingered so long. One by one, the doubting family turned to faith.
p190.s2.b5: When James rushed into the house crying that he had seen his brother, the family began at last to believe in the resurrection. He announced that he would not return to Galilee, and David, remarking that not only excited women but strong men were beginning to see him, hoped to see him too. Because of something said to him in the garden, James asked that this visit not be widely reported, and he allowed only Mary Magdalene to return to Joseph’s home.
p190.s2.b6: There is something moving in the fact that the brother who had watched Jesus closely all his life and yet failed to believe received the first personal visit of the risen Jesus. Jesus did not rebuke his doubt; he called him by name and invited him to serve. Those closest to us may be slowest to believe, but the door stays open to the end.
p190.s3.h: III–IV. At the Home of Joseph; Appearance to the Greeks — A Kingdom Without Distinction
p190.s3.b0: The fifth appearance came at about a quarter past four that afternoon, before some twenty-five women believers gathered at the home of Joseph of Arimathea. As Mary Magdalene was telling what had happened at Bethany, a solemn hush fell, and Jesus stood among them. He gave the women, too, the commission to proclaim the gospel to all the world.
p190.s3.b2: At about the same time, at the home of Flavius, some forty Greek believers were discussing the news of the resurrection behind fastened doors. In his sixth appearance Jesus came among them and said that the Son of Man had appeared among the Jews but had come to minister to all men. Many of them had been at Gethsemane when Jesus was arrested.
p190.s3.b4: Mary Magdalene had witnessed four of the five appearances made so far. The Greeks were so overcome with awe and fear that none of them slept that night; they stayed awake talking of these things and hoping the Master would come again. That women and gentiles were among the earliest witnesses of the risen Lord matches perfectly the message of a kingdom without distinctions that he proclaimed.
p190.s3.b5: Meanwhile the Sanhedrin, disturbed by the rumors of resurrection, met that evening and decided to expel from the synagogue anyone who spoke of it. They thought they were finished with Jesus, but the text says their real trouble was only beginning. Jesus left the apostles a few more hours for reflection before visiting them.
p190.s4.h: V. The Walk with Two Brothers — Hearts That Burned Within
p190.s4.b0: Cleopas and Jacob, shepherd brothers from Emmaus, were walking home arguing about the reports of the empty tomb. The elder was half inclined to believe; the younger insisted it was a fraud. In his seventh appearance the morontia Jesus walked beside them, but even Cleopas, who had often eaten with him, did not recognize him.
p190.s4.b1: Asked what they were discussing, Cleopas said he must be the only one in Jerusalem who did not know, and he told the story: a prophet mighty in word and deed had been crucified; many had hoped he would be Israel’s deliverer; and that day women had reported an empty tomb and a conversation with him. Jacob added that the two apostles who went to the tomb had not seen Jesus.
p190.s4.b2: Jesus said he knew that man’s teachings better than anyone and set about enlightening them. He reminded them that the kingdom was not of this world, that Jesus had foretold he would rise on the third day, and he went one by one through the promises of a deliverer in the Scriptures.

p190.s4.b5: At their door the brothers urged him to stay, and as he began to break the bread and hand it to them, their eyes were opened. The moment Cleopas said it was the Master, he vanished. Without eating, the two hurried back to Jerusalem to tell the apostles in the upper room.
p190.s4.b7: The brothers had already been stirred by the teaching on the road, but their eyes were opened only when they sat together and shared bread. Understanding the truth and recognizing him as a person do not always come at the same moment. A small act of hospitality, urging a stranger to stay, made room for that recognition.
p190.s5.b0: Paper 190 follows the single day of the resurrection Sunday. On that day Jesus appeared first to those who had doubted most and to those most often overlooked: his brother James, the women, the Greeks, and two shepherds on the road. And the first to carry the news through the land were lay messengers.

p191.lead: Ten apostles behind bolted doors, Peter forgiven, Thomas laying down his doubts: two weeks in which the risen Master visited the apostles and the believers of Philadelphia and Alexandria.

p191.foot.text: Narrated by a secondary midwayer once assigned to the Apostle Andrew

p191.s0.h: Introduction — A Resurrection Day Behind Bolted Doors
p191.s0.b0: Resurrection Sunday was a terrible day for the apostles. Fearing arrest by agents of the Sanhedrin, the ten spent it in the upper room with the doors bolted. Thomas brooded alone at Bethpage. The text remarks that he would have fared much better had he stayed with his fellows.
p191.s0.b1: Their isolation made things harder. David’s messengers, who had always brought them news from outside, had all gone off to announce the resurrection. John Mark brought rumors and reports from around the temple, but it did not occur to him to gather news from the groups of believers to whom Jesus had already appeared. For the first time the apostles realized how much they had depended on David’s messengers.
p191.s0.b2: The text portrays the minds of the ten one by one on that day. Faced with the same news, each reacted according to his own temperament. The scene shows how differently a crisis of faith can come to different people.

p191.s0.b4: Jesus had reasons for delaying his first appearance to the apostles. He wanted them to reflect on his forecasts, he wanted Peter to wrestle through his difficulties, and he wanted Thomas to be with them. Thomas’s pride kept him from returning on his own; the apostles waited for him, and he waited for them to come for him. So they would not leave for Galilee without Thomas.
p191.s1.h: I. The Appearance to Peter — Forgiven Before He Asked
p191.s1.b0: About half past eight that evening, Jesus appeared to Peter in the garden of the Mark home. It was his eighth morontia manifestation. Since his denial, Peter had been fighting the fear that he might no longer be an apostle, and he wondered whether his presence was keeping Jesus from coming to the others.
p191.s1.b1: He thought of the Master’s loving look as he passed by on Annas’s porch, and of the women’s message, “⟦Q 191:0.4⟧Go tell my apostles—and Peter.⟦/Q⟧” His faith began to surmount his doubts, and he declared aloud that he believed. Just then the Master spoke to him in familiar tones.
p191.s1.b4: Forgiveness did not stop at covering the past; it led straight into a new task. To stop thinking about oneself and one’s troubles and to think instead of what one can give to others is the most practical remedy for a person bound by guilt. Peter ran to the upper room crying that the Master had forgiven him. But when Andrew hinted at the vision of the night Peter walked on the water, he was crestfallen, and only the twins came to him saying they believed him.
p191.s2.h: II. First Appearance to the Apostles — Faith in One Another
p191.s2.b0: Shortly after nine, with all the doors bolted, the Master appeared in the upper room. It was his ninth appearance. He asked whether he had not told them, while still in the flesh, of his betrayal, his death, and his rising on the third day, and he pointed to the doubts with which they had argued over the reports of the women, the Emmaus brothers, and Peter.
p191.s2.b2: Jesus reminded them that one of them was absent, and told them to go into Galilee once they were all together and certain. Setting faith in one another beside faith in God is significant, for that was exactly what these brothers needed, having just belittled Peter’s testimony.
p191.s3.h: III. With the Morontia Creatures — The Seventh Bestowal Completed
p191.s3.b0: The next day, Monday, Jesus spent with the morontia creatures present on Urantia. More than a million morontia directors and associates, together with transition mortals from the mansion worlds of Satania, were taking part in his transition experience. He taught them, and he also learned from the directors about the morontia career that mortals pass through on the mansion worlds.
p191.s3.b1: About midnight that Monday his form was adjusted to the second morontia stage. The higher the stage, the more difficult it became to make him visible to mortal eyes. His later progress is recorded by date.

Morontia progress

p191.s3.b4: In his previous bestowals Michael had already experienced to the full the life of ascending mortals, but with his morontia experience on Urantia he completed his service of universe experience. That the Creator has gone ahead of us on the mansion-world path we will one day walk is a great comfort for the ascending journey.
p191.s4.h: IV. The Tenth Appearance (At Philadelphia) — Disciples Who Love One Another
p191.s4.b0: On the evening of Tuesday, April 11, Jesus appeared in the synagogue at Philadelphia to about one hundred and fifty believers, among them Abner, Lazarus, and more than fifty of the seventy evangelists. It was his tenth appearance. With the resurrected Lazarus among them, they found the report of the resurrection easy to believe. Apart from the five hundred in Galilee, this was the largest group to see him at one time.
p191.s4.b2: Jesus said there is but one gospel, and urged them to fellowship all their brethren who proclaim it, whether Jew, Greek, or Persian. His question — if you are ennobled to love unbelievers, should you not love your fellow believers just as much? — still speaks to communities of faith today. The next morning they went out at once to proclaim the resurrection.
p191.s4.b3: On the following Wednesday Jesus again spent the day with his morontia associates. In the afternoon he received morontia delegates from the mansion worlds throughout the constellation of Norlatiadek. They rejoiced to know their Creator as a universe intelligence of their own order. That the Creator had come down to the place of the creature and walked with them was a joy even to heavenly beings.
p191.s5.h: V. Second Appearance to the Apostles — Those Who Believe Without Seeing
p191.s5.b0: Thomas spent a lonely week in the hills around Olivet, and on Saturday night two apostles brought him back. Even then he refused to believe, claiming Peter had excited the others. The text analyzes his doubt delicately: it was tangled with emotional stubbornness and embarrassment at having run away, and he unconsciously enjoyed the attention of his fellows.
p191.s5.b1: At supper the next evening, when he said he would not believe unless he could touch the nail marks, the Master appeared right before him. Jesus first renewed the commission to them all: as the Father had sent him, so he sent them, and they were to reveal divine love not only in words but in daily living.
p191.s5.b3: Jesus told them that for now they were hiding their light behind closed doors out of fear, but that when baptized with the Spirit of Truth they would go forth bravely and joyously. He called this change the shock of the transition from the false security of the authority of traditionalism to the authority of faith in living experience. He knew that letting go of a familiar authority to stand on experienced truth is not easy, and so he allowed them time to recover.

What they prized

p191.s5.b5: Then Jesus turned to Thomas. He said there were no nail marks on his hands because he had been raised in the form Thomas himself would have, and he told him that even while he was stoutly asserting his unbelief, he had already begun to believe in his heart.
p191.s5.b8: Thomas fell on his knees and confessed, “⟦Q 191:5.5⟧My Lord and my Master!⟦/Q⟧” Now the eleven were fully convinced, and before dawn the next day they set out for Galilee. That final blessing is addressed less to Thomas than to today’s reader, for we are the very people of the ages to come, called to believe without seeing.
p191.s6.h: VI. The Alexandrian Appearance — A Gospel That Belongs to All
p191.s6.b0: On the evening of April 18, as the apostles were nearing Galilee, Jesus appeared at Alexandria to Rodan and some eighty believers. It was his twelfth appearance. It came at the very moment Nathan of Busiris was finishing his account of the crucifixion with David’s report that the Master had said he would rise again.
p191.s6.b2: Jesus told them the gospel belongs not to any one race or group of teachers but to all who believe, little children included. When David’s herald of the resurrection arrived two days later with the news, they answered that they already knew.
p191.s7.b0: In Paper 191 the risen Jesus lifts up broken people one at a time. Peter, who had denied him, received forgiveness along with a task; Thomas, who had doubted, received understanding rather than rebuke. And the words he gave to the apostles, to Philadelphia, and to Alexandria come together in one message: a life of loving and serving people as he loved and served them is itself the proclamation of the gospel.

Grow a faith that believes without seeing
Blessed are those who believe without seeing (191:5.5)

p191.s7.b3: In the next paper, Paper 192, “⟦Q 191:4.5⟧Appearances in Galilee,⟦/Q⟧” the apostles meet the Master again by the lake of their home country, and Peter faces three questions.
p192.lead: Breakfast by the home lake, last counsel given while walking two by two, rededication on the mount of ordination — and the moment the religion of Jesus began to become a religion about Jesus.

p192.foot.text: Narrated by a secondary midwayer once assigned to the Apostle Andrew

p192.s0.b0: By the time the apostles left for Galilee, the Jewish leaders had grown quiet. Since Jesus appeared only to believers and the apostles were in hiding, the rulers concluded that the gospel movement had been crushed. They were troubled by the spreading rumors of resurrection, but they counted on the bribed guards to say that the followers had removed the body.
p192.s0.b1: From this time Peter became the recognized head of the apostolic group. Jesus had never given him this authority, nor had his fellows formally chosen him. Because he was the chief preacher, he took the place naturally and by common consent, for public preaching had now become the apostles’ chief work. Later Matthias, who took Judas’s place, became treasurer.
p192.s0.b2: When the apostles set out on Monday morning, young John Mark followed them secretly and only openly joined them well beyond Bethany. They stopped several times along the way to tell of the risen Master and did not reach Bethsaida until late Wednesday night.
p192.s1.h: I. Appearance by the Lake — Not a Miracle but Foreknowledge, and a Charcoal Fire
p192.s1.b0: At Peter’s suggestion the apostles fished all night but caught nothing. They did not mind, for they had much to talk about. About six o’clock on the morning of Friday, April 21, as they were coming back to shore, a man standing by a fire called to them to cast the net on the right side. When the net filled, John, quicker of perception, recognized the Master, and Peter plunged at once into the water. It was the first appearance in Galilee and the thirteenth in all.
p192.s1.b1: The apostles did not fully understand why Jesus wanted to meet them in Galilee rather than Jerusalem. The text explains that he wished to meet them away from the confined surroundings charged with memories of fear, betrayal, and death, out in the open nature where they had once lived together. He knew the power of a place to heal wounded hearts.
p192.s1.b2: There was a simple reason they did not recognize him at first. Asking fishermen on the beach what they had caught was the customary greeting of the fish dealers from Tarichea who came down to buy the fresh catch. The text paints even this resurrection scene in the texture of ordinary life.
p192.s1.b3: There were 153 large fish. The text says plainly that it is a mistake to call this another miraculous catch.
p192.s1.b5: John Mark, seeing eleven men instead of ten, ran ahead and knelt at the Master’s feet. Unlike the solemn greeting in Jerusalem, Jesus welcomed him in commonplace tones. Peter, meanwhile, was shaken at the sight of the charcoal fire on the beach, which brought back the fire in Annas’s courtyard on the night he denied his Master. But he gathered himself and fell at the Master’s feet.
p192.s1.b7: Jesus had them cook the fish and break the bread, and at the end he himself served the lad. Then he talked of all they had been through together by that lake. That the risen Master’s first act was to give breakfast to weary men shows how concrete and human his ministry was. And for Simon Zelotes, who had gone home discouraged, Jesus sent Peter and Andrew to bring him back that very day.
p192.s2.h: II. Visiting with the Apostles Two and Two — A Different Question for Each
p192.s2.b0: After breakfast Jesus walked along the beach with the apostles two by two. He did not say the same thing to everyone. Some he asked whether they loved him; others, whether they believed in him, served him, or obeyed him. And he gave each counsel fitted exactly to his weaknesses and his future.

head: Apostle
Question
Heart of the counsel
rows: Give up your intolerance and prove by your life that love is the greatest thing
Feed my lambs, care for the flock, and follow me to the end
Trust your brethren more, Peter included, and become the counselor of my brother James
The more you trust, the less impatient you will be; cultivate patience
Cease your doubting and grow in faith and the knowledge of truth
Mix friendship with your counsel, add love to your philosophy, and be less critical
Go to the lands of the gentiles and proclaim the gospel without fear
Have you in your heart to obey me?
Teach the good news of spiritual salvation rather than material provision
If you return to your former work, remember that all upright work is sacred

p192.s2.b3: Peter was asked the same question three times. The third time he was grieved, feeling that the Master seemed to distrust him, but each time Jesus answered with a commission to care for his flock. The man who had denied him three times received three confessions and three commissions. The last charge shows clearly the pattern of the shepherd.
p192.s2.b5: When Peter asked what would become of John, Jesus told him not to be concerned about his brethren’s future. This saying spread as meaning that John would not die before the Master’s return, and that interpretation actually did much to bring Simon Zelotes back to service.
p192.s2.b6: The words to Andrew were for one who had laid down a place of leadership. Once in charge of directing his brethren, he now had to trust others more, even his brother Peter. Foreseeing that when persecution scattered the apostles, his brother James would bear a burden his experience could hardly carry, Jesus asked Andrew to become his counselor. It shows that great service is possible even from a place one has stepped back from.
p192.s2.b9: Thomas was told to believe like a child but to stop acting childishly. The twins were told that even if their outward work changed, their allegiance must not waver. This charge is the one nearest to most believers, who live ordinary everyday lives.
p192.s2.b10: Philip and Matthew had long looked after money, supplies, and the material needs of their brethren. Jesus told them they were now as free as the others to proclaim the good news; the only law they had to obey was the command to go forth and preach the gospel. James Zebedee he told to weigh the results of his words and deeds and to pray for calmness of spirit, and he foreshadowed the time when James would drink the cup of sacrifice.
p192.s3.h: III. On the Mount of Ordination — A Pledge Renewed
p192.s3.b0: At noon on Saturday, April 22, the eleven gathered on the hill near Capernaum where they had first been ordained. It was the fourteenth appearance. They knelt in a circle about the Master, and Jesus repeated the original charges and re-enacted the ordination scene.
p192.s3.b1: Everything was as they remembered it except the prayer. It was spoken in tones of majesty and power such as the apostles had never heard. The eleven never forgot this experience of rededication.
p192.s3.b2: To return to the place of their first ordination and renew the same pledge was to confirm that, even after failure and scattering, their calling had not been withdrawn. On the path of faith too, going back to the place of one’s first dedication and renewing one’s heart can give great strength.
p192.s3.b4: For a whole week afterward no one saw Jesus. Unsure whether he had gone to the Father, the apostles stayed at Bethsaida and did not even go fishing for fear of missing him. During that time Jesus was occupied with the morontia creatures in the affairs of his morontia transition.
p192.s4.h: IV. The Lakeside Gathering and After — The Center of the Message Shifts
p192.s4.b0: As news of the appearances spread through Galilee, Peter announced a public meeting for the Sabbath afternoon. On Saturday, April 29, more than five hundred believers gathered at Bethsaida to hear his first public sermon since the resurrection. Just as he finished his declaration, the Master appeared beside him, wished them peace, and vanished. It was the fifteenth appearance.
p192.s4.b2: The apostles returned to Jerusalem, and John Mark lost his father, Elijah Mark, a few hours before they arrived. The assurance of the resurrection comforted them, but they felt deeply the loss of a staunch friend. The upper room of the Mark home remained their headquarters until after Pentecost.
p192.s4.b3: That Thursday night the apostles, except Thomas, Simon Zelotes, and the twins, pledged themselves to proclaim publicly the new gospel of the risen Lord. Nathaniel objected to shifting the center of the message, but he could not withstand Peter’s eloquence and the enthusiasm of the believers.

head: Point
The gospel Jesus preached
The message the apostles now put first
rows: Sonship with God and brotherhood with man
Driven by the enthusiasm of Peter and the women believers

p192.s4.b6: The text calls those who did this well-meaning representatives; it was enthusiasm, not ill will, that drove the change. Here the reader may ask himself or herself: am I holding beliefs about Jesus, or am I living the faith that Jesus lived?
p192.s5.b0: The Jesus of Paper 192 chooses breakfast over miracles and questions fitted to each person over rebuke. In nine walks he named each apostle’s weakness precisely, yet wrapped it in a promise for the future. And the paper ends by quietly recording the crossroads at which the center of the gospel began to shift.
p192.s5.b1: What the reader gains from this paper is respect for individuality. Jesus asked each person a different question, and each question pointed exactly to where that person most needed to grow. We too can consider what he would ask us: Do you love me? Do you trust me? Do you serve me? Do you obey me?

head: Appearance
Time and place
To whom
rows: Friday dawn, April 21, by the lake at Bethsaida
Saturday noon, April 22, the mount of ordination
Saturday afternoon, April 29, the seaside at Bethsaida

head: Practice
The teaching behind it
rows: Offer the weary a warm meal first
Bow again even when memories of failure return
Follow your own path without comparing yourself to others
Only make sure that you follow me (192:2.5)
Add friendship to advice and love to your thinking
Do everyday work as for God
Nothing a son of God does can be common (192:2.13)
Live the faith of Jesus rather than beliefs about him
The religion of Jesus and the religion about Jesus (192:4.8)

p192.s5.b4: In the next paper, Paper 193, “Final Appearances and Ascension,” Jesus leaves his last counsel and ascends to the Father from Olivet.
p193.lead: The resurrection is not the gospel but a result of it: the last four appearances, the lesson in isolation left by Judas’s downfall, and the farewell on Olivet.

p193.foot.text: Narrated by a secondary midwayer once assigned to the Apostle Andrew

p193.s0.h: Introduction — The Last Great Teaching in Nicodemus’s Courtyard
p193.s0.b0: On Friday night, May 5, the believers in Jerusalem gathered together for the first time since the resurrection. The eleven apostles, the women’s corps, about fifty leading disciples, and a few Greeks were in the courtyard of Nicodemus. Jesus appeared there in his sixteenth appearance, called it the most representative group yet, gathering apostles and disciples, men and women, and began at once to teach.
p193.s0.b1: He asked first why they were so surprised. He had spoken plainly of his death and resurrection, but they had heard his words without grasping their meaning. So now he urged them not to repeat the mistake of hearing with the mind and failing to understand with the heart. And he declared again that his one purpose had been to reveal the Father to his children.
p193.s0.b2: Here Jesus drew a clear line against the change the apostles had just begun — the move to put the proclamation of the resurrection at the center of the message. Their mission was still to proclaim the fatherhood of God and the sonship of man, and to preach the whole truth of the gospel, not a part of it.
p193.s0.b4: He said there was nothing strange in his having risen, for the Father gives his Paradise Sons the power to lay down life and take it up again. Something else, rather, should stir their hearts.
p193.s0.b6: Jesus told them that as he had revealed God by loving and serving them, so they could reveal God to their fellows through loving service. And he told them to remain in Jerusalem until the Spirit of Truth came. The believers stayed until dawn discussing his counsel.
p193.s1.h: I–II. The Appearance at Sychar; The Phoenician Appearance — Faith and the Fruits of the Spirit
p193.s1.b0: On the Sabbath afternoon of May 13, Jesus appeared near Jacob’s well at Sychar to Nalda and about seventy-five Samaritan believers. It was his seventeenth appearance. He said that rejoicing to know him as the resurrection and the life would avail nothing unless they were first born of the spirit and possessed eternal life by faith. And he said the time had come to worship God neither on Gerizim nor at Jerusalem, but where they were, as they were, in spirit and in truth.
p193.s1.b2: He added that salvation is a free gift, yet it is followed by the experience of bearing the fruits of the spirit life lived in the flesh. To accept the fatherhood of God is also to accept the brotherhood of man. A brother is even more than a neighbor: one to be loved with family affection and served as one would serve oneself.
p193.s1.b3: On Tuesday evening, May 16, came the eighteenth appearance, at Tyre. Here Jesus spoke words that are the key to this paper. Resurrection and survival are great facts related to the gospel, but they are only part of the result of believing the good news.
p193.s1.b5: He then named one by one the fruits borne in the lives of spirit-born, God-knowing mortals. The list is a mirror in which believers can examine their own lives. Professed believers who do not bear these fruits, he said sternly, are useless branches on the living vine.
p193.s1.b8: The believers at Tyre had known Jesus in the flesh, and they recognized him as soon as he began to speak. The text says that though his friends did not easily recognize the morontia form, they were never slow to recognize his personality. The next day the news spread to Sidon, Antioch, and Damascus.
p193.s2.h: III. Last Appearance in Jerusalem — Do Not Be Alone
p193.s2.b0: On Thursday morning, May 18, Jesus made his last morontia appearance on earth to the eleven apostles as they were about to breakfast in the upper room. Simon Zelotes asked whether he would now restore the kingdom, and Jesus replied that he still clung to his old ideas of a material kingdom.
p193.s2.b1: Just before leaving them, Jesus urged them again to love and trust one another. Judas was no longer with them, he said, because his love had grown cold and he had refused to trust his brethren. He explained that he had sent them out two and two, and had not allowed himself to be alone for long periods while in the flesh, precisely to guard against the mischief of isolation.
p193.s2.b3: Jesus pointed to his own example. From the beginning of their association he had always kept two or three of them by his side, even when he communed with the Father. That the one most deeply united with God did not make light of human companionship tells us that the spiritual life is not a path of solitary isolation. Because he was leaving them alone in the world that very day, this charge was all the more urgent.
p193.s2.b4: When he had finished, he led the apostles out to Olivet. From the time they left the upper room until they stopped on the mountain, no one spoke a word.
p193.s3.h: IV. Causes of Judas’s Downfall — How Isolation Destroys
p193.s3.b0: At the beginning of his farewell message Jesus held up Judas as a solemn warning against the dangers of social and fraternal isolation. In the light of those words and of the centuries of enlightenment since, the narrator reviews the causes of Judas’s downfall. The chief reason was that he was a markedly isolated personality. Yet isolation alone would not have done such harm; he also failed to grow in love and spiritual grace, and he nursed grudges and a craving for revenge.

head: What brought Judas down
The text’s explanation
rows: He chose to grow up as an individualistic and unsocial person
He resented being thwarted and could not stand to lose
Instead of accepting disappointment as a common feature of life, he blamed others
He was always thinking of revenge
He would not share his personal problems with true friends or with the Master
He never learned that the true reward of noble living is a spiritual one

p193.s3.b2: The text states plainly that Judas need not have gone wrong. Thomas and Nathaniel had the same kind of suspicion and overdeveloped individualism, and Andrew and Matthew had similar leanings. The difference was that over time they grew in love and trust. Judas, by contrast, whenever his conflicts piled up, sought consolation not from his brethren but from those who were indifferent or hostile to the kingdom.
p193.s3.b6: The narrator says this analysis is meant not to condemn Judas but to help believers today. The habit of blaming someone for our disappointments, and the stubborn refusal to confide in those close to us, can be found in anyone. The remedy is simple: trust our brethren more, and slowly develop the ability to confide in them.
p193.s4.h: V. The Master’s Ascension — Farewell on Olivet
p193.s4.b0: About half past seven that morning Jesus and the eleven reached the western slope of Olivet, overlooking Jerusalem and Gethsemane. Without being told, the apostles knelt in a circle about him. Jesus urged them once more to remain in Jerusalem until they were endowed with power from on high, and he left them his last words.
p193.s4.b2: About a quarter to eight he vanished from their sight. The text does not dramatize the scene. It says plainly that the so-called ascension was no different from the other times he had disappeared from view during the forty days.
p193.s4.b4: The journey that followed is recorded on a universe scale. The Master went by way of Jerusem to Edentia, where the Most Highs released him from morontia status and restored him to the status of a Paradise Son and the supreme sovereignty of Salvington. He went on to the right hand of the Father to receive formal confirmation of his completed sovereignty of Nebadon.
p193.s5.h: VI. Peter Calls a Meeting — The Twelve Disperse
p193.s5.b0: At half past ten, one hundred and twenty of the leading disciples in Jerusalem gathered at the home of Mary Mark. Jesus’ mother Mary and his brother James were there. Peter gave a moving report of the last meeting and the farewell; this was the first council the disciples held after the end of the Master’s planetary career.
p193.s5.b2: The apostles chose Matthias by lot to succeed Judas, though he took little part in their later work. After Pentecost the twins returned to Galilee, Simon Zelotes withdrew for a time, and Nathaniel, parting from Peter over preaching about Jesus, went to Philadelphia and on beyond Mesopotamia. Only six — Peter, Andrew, James, John, Philip, and Matthew — remained on the scene of the first proclamation in Jerusalem.
p193.s6.b0: Paper 193 closes Jesus’ life on earth. In his last appearances he stressed the same thing again and again: the resurrection is a result of the gospel, not the gospel itself, and the gospel is the fatherhood of God and the brotherhood of man. And that gospel is carried less by words than by a life that bears the fruits of the spirit.

head: Appearance
Time and place
To whom
rows: Friday night, May 5, the courtyard of Nicodemus
A representative group of apostles, women, and disciples
Sabbath afternoon, May 13, Jacob’s well at Sychar
Thursday morning, May 18, the upper room and Olivet

head: Practice
The teaching behind it
rows: Center your faith on the gospel of sonship rather than the resurrection
Worship in spirit and truth wherever you are
Neither on Gerizim nor at Jerusalem (193:1.2)
Examine your faith by the fruits of the spirit
Confide in those close to you
Trust and confide in one another (193:3.2)
Do not blame others for your disappointments
Do not look for reward in this life alone

p193.s6.b3: In the next paper, Paper 194, “Bestowal of the Spirit of Truth,” the promised spirit is poured out upon all flesh at Pentecost.
p194.lead: The Spirit of Truth poured out at Pentecost: a new teacher who reveals the Creator Son in the heart, a liberation that erased every distinction, and the beginnings of the church as a religion about Jesus.

p194.foot.text: Narrated by a secondary midwayer once assigned to the Apostle Andrew

p194.s0.h: Introduction — A Strange Presence in the Upper Room
p194.s0.b0: About one o’clock on the day of Pentecost, the one hundred and twenty believers at prayer became aware of a strange presence in the room. They were conscious of a new and profound sense of spiritual joy, security, and confidence, and soon afterward they felt a strong urge to go out and proclaim the gospel publicly. Peter declared that this was the promised Spirit of Truth and proposed that they go to the temple.
p194.s0.b1: They had been trained to preach the fatherhood of God and the sonship of man, but in their moment of triumph the greatest news they could think of was the risen Master. Here the narrator points out the crossroads that would shape all later history.

head: Message
What it combined
rows: The fact of the fatherhood of God + the truth of the sonship-brotherhood of men that follows from it
Christianity as it developed from that day
The fact of God as the Father of the Lord Jesus Christ + the experience of fellowship with the risen and glorified Christ

p194.s0.b4: The text seeks to understand this change rather than to scold it. In their triumph over the forces that had sought to destroy their Master, and in their overwhelming assurance that he lived and their friendship was not ended, it is easy to see how they came to preach a new gospel about Jesus. This generous view is worth imitating when we read church history.
p194.s1.h: I. The Pentecost Sermon — From Hiding to the Temple
p194.s1.b0: After forty days in hiding, the apostles appeared boldly in the temple, crowded for the feast of Pentecost. About two o’clock Peter made a fervent appeal from the very spot where the Master had last taught, and more than two thousand souls responded. For more than an hour and a half six apostles proclaimed the message in Greek, Hebrew, and Aramaic.
p194.s1.b1: The Jewish leaders were astonished at their boldness, but so many believed that they dared not interfere. At half past four the new believers went down to the pool of Siloam to be baptized, and the work was not finished until after dark. Yet they had not broken away from Judaism; for a time those who believed in Jesus remained a sect within it.
p194.s2.h: II. The Significance of Pentecost — What the Spirit of Truth Does
p194.s2.b0: Jesus’ message was an effective solvent for the spiritual difficulties of the people of his day. The Spirit of Truth, sent after his departure, restates that message for each new generation, so that every age has its own new version of the gospel. Truth is not bound to the forms of one age; it comes alive anew in each generation.

head: Mission of the Spirit of Truth
The text’s explanation
rows: To foster and personalize truth — the comprehension of truth is the highest form of liberty
To destroy the believer’s feeling of being orphaned
To prepare all normal minds for the universal bestowal of Adjusters
To help believers remember the Master’s words and to illuminate and reinterpret his life
To help them bear witness to Jesus’ life as lived anew in them
To lead them into all truth, into the knowledge of ascending sonship with God

p194.s2.b2: The text corrects a common misunderstanding. Do not expect to become strongly conscious of the Spirit of Truth in your intellect. The spirit creates a consciousness not of himself but of Michael, the Son.
p194.s2.b5: His life and death soon became a new gospel of ransom. Yet the text says that even this greatly distorted message carried many of the fundamental truths of the gospel of the kingdom, and that the concealed truths of the fatherhood of God and the brotherhood of men will one day emerge to transform civilization. Nor did these intellectual errors block spiritual growth: within a month of the spirit’s coming, the apostles made more spiritual progress than in almost four years with the Master.
p194.s2.b6: Man now receives a threefold spirit endowment: the spirit of the Father in the Thought Adjuster, the spirit of the Son in the Spirit of Truth, and the spirit of the Spirit in the Holy Spirit. The text goes on to list seven higher spirit influences that rest upon a progressing humanity.

head: Seven spirits of the advancing worlds
Description
rows: 1. The bestowed spirit of the Universal Father
2. The spirit presence of the Eternal Son
The spirit gravity of the universe of universes, the channel of all spirit communion
3. The spirit presence of the Infinite Spirit
The universal spirit-mind of all creation
4. The spirit of the Universal Father and the Creator Son
5. The spirit of the Infinite Spirit and the Universe Mother Spirit
6. The mind-spirit of the Universe Mother Spirit
The seven adjutant mind-spirits of the local universe
7. The spirit of the Father, Sons, and Spirits
The new-name spirit of ascending mortals who have fused with their Adjusters and attained finaliter status

p194.s3.h: III. What Happened at Pentecost — God Seeking Man
p194.s3.b0: In later times Pentecost was confused with outbursts of rampant emotionalism. But the chief mission of the outpoured spirit is to teach the truths of the Father’s love and the Son’s mercy. When people bear the fruits of the spirit, they are simply showing forth the traits the Master manifested in his own earthly life.
p194.s3.b2: In a world where sin seems to win, does faith finally prevail? The text answers yes. The day of the cross was dark, but the resurrection morning was bright, and Pentecost brighter still. The religion of Jesus is not a means of escape from life; it is a religion of faith, hope, and love that exalts the life we now live in the flesh.
p194.s3.b4: Pentecost was a liberation on many levels. Gathering what the text lists in turn shows how many fetters the gift of the spirit loosed from religion.

head: What Pentecost set free
The text’s explanation
rows: It broke all national limitations and racial fetters
True religion finds its manifestation in the individual soul
It detached spiritual experience from the idea of especially favorable environments
It armed believers with the spiritual weapons of forgiveness, good will, and love
Woman stands before God on an equality with man
Even Jesus’ own family received no more than others

p194.s3.b7: The text stresses that the Spirit of Truth did not come to the apostles alone. All one hundred and twenty men and women in the upper room received the new teacher, as did all the honest of heart throughout the world. Each soul received him according to its love of truth and its capacity to grasp spiritual realities. Since the same thing happened at the same time to the believers at Philadelphia and Alexandria, the company of believers was truly of one heart and soul.
p194.s3.b8: The text says that Pentecost made possible a religion neither radical nor conservative. Jesus’ earth life is the fixed point that anchors it in time, while the Spirit of Truth enables it to grow without end. Pentecost was also designed to lessen the self-assertion of individuals, nations, and races. Amid destructive wars, the one conqueror whose fame has grown is the gospel of Jesus, which overcomes evil with good.
p194.s3.b10: Prayer, too, is put in its proper place. Prayer did not bring the spirit, but it had much to do with the capacity of receptivity of each believer. Prayer does not move God’s heart to give more; it digs deeper channels through which the divine bestowals may flow. The apostles’ experience, likewise, was not an emotional outburst but an intelligent self-surrender.
p194.s4.h: IV. Beginnings of the Christian Church — From the Brotherhood of Jesus to the Church
p194.s4.b0: The apostles, broken before the cross, were delivered from despair by the resurrection, and with the new teacher of Pentecost they became bold followers of a living Lord. The text sums up the change in a single sentence.
p194.s4.b2: The early community was simple. They met daily in the temple and broke bread in their homes, ending their common meals with the Lord’s Supper. At first they baptized in the name of Jesus, and baptism was the only requirement. It was simply the brotherhood of Jesus, without organization.
p194.s4.b3: But the message had become the gospel of the Lord Jesus Christ. The fact of his first coming and the hope of his soon second coming became the center of their preaching. A marvelous brotherly love sprang up in these communities, but it was a fellowship of believers in Jesus, not of brothers in the family of the Father in heaven.

head: Stage
What happened
rows: No organization; admission by baptism alone, in the name of Jesus
Voluntary sharing in expectation of the second coming — ending in sorrow when resources ran out
The Sadducees withdrew, and a period of peace followed
Disciples of Rodan won Stephen, Barnabas, and others
Organized within a month under Peter’s leadership, with James as nominal head
Called Christianity at Antioch, it spread to the ends of the empire

p194.s4.b6: The experiment in common ownership did not come directly from Jesus’ teaching; it grew out of the conviction that his return was imminent. The text frankly records that this unthinking brotherly love ended in calamity and sorrow. Good motives, without wisdom, do not bear fruit.
p194.s5.b0: Paper 194 shows two things together. One is the glory of Pentecost, in which God seeks out man and dwells within him; the other is the human limitation that mistook the results of the gospel for the gospel itself. Yet because the Spirit of Truth restates Jesus’ message for every generation, the concealed truths of the fatherhood of God and the brotherhood of men can always emerge again.

head: Practice
The teaching behind it
rows: Recognize the spirit’s work in a deepening fellowship with Michael
Submit to the Father’s will rather than imitate Jesus outwardly
Hold a faith that exalts life instead of escaping it
Welcome the spirit here and now, not in special places or forms
Dig deeper channels of receptivity through prayer
Discriminations of sex, race, and caste erased (194:3.14)

p194.s5.b2: The next paper, Paper 195, “After Pentecost,” traces how Christianity spread through the Roman world and the challenges religion faces in the modern world.
p195.lead: How Christianity won the Greco-Roman world and survived the Dark Ages, and why, in an age of materialism and secularism, the religion of Jesus must be rediscovered.

p195.foot.text: Narrated by a secondary midwayer once assigned to the Apostle Andrew

p195.s0.h: Introduction — A Victory Won by Compromise
p195.s0.b0: Paper 195 surveys nearly two thousand years of history after Pentecost and then turns to the problems of the modern world. Peter was the real founder of the church, Paul carried the message to the gentiles, and Greek believers spread it through the empire. The Hebrews as a nation did not accept it, but the Western world — intellectual, weary of war, and skeptical of its existing religions — was hungry for a religion that would satisfy the soul.
p195.s0.b1: The conflict between the new message and the old order ended in compromise. Christianity did not remain the simple spiritual appeal of Jesus; it emerged as a new social order embracing ritual, law, government, and morals. The text names five reasons why a message that had nearly failed in its birthplace captured the best minds of the empire.

head: Why Christianity triumphed
What happened
rows: Paul was a great organizer, and his successors kept up the pace
It embraced the best in Greek philosophy and the cream of Hebrew theology
The echo of Jesus’ life bestowal and a message of salvation for all mankind
It drew in the better half of its adherents
It won over even the emperor Constantine

p195.s0.b3: The old order won many small victories in ritual. But Christianity gained the upper hand in four things: a higher moral standard, a greatly enlarged concept of God, the hope of immortality made a religious assurance, and Jesus of Nazareth offered to hungry souls. The text adds that had Athanasius not stood firm at Nicaea, the truth of Jesus’ bestowal might have been obscured.
p195.s1.h: I–II. Influence of the Greeks; The Roman Influence — Two Peoples Who Loved Truth
p195.s1.b0: Hellenization began in earnest the day Paul spoke before the council of the Areopagus in Athens about “⟦Q 195:1.1⟧the Unknown God.⟦/Q⟧” Greek philosophy and Jesus’ teaching shared a goal: the emergence of the individual. The Greeks taught intellectual freedom leading to political liberty; Jesus taught spiritual freedom leading to religious liberty. Together they became a new charter of human freedom.
p195.s1.b2: The Greeks earnestly debated every human problem except religion, while the Jews neglected every other field and took their religion very seriously, too seriously. Illuminated by Jesus’ message, the union of these two streams became the driving power of a new social order. By contrast, the Abnerian branch in the east, more faithful to Jesus’ teachings, refused to compromise, made little headway, and was finally lost in the Islamic movement.
p195.s1.b3: Rome brought tolerance of foreign languages, peoples, and religions. The early persecutions arose largely because the Christians’ use of the word “kingdom” was taken as political rivalry. To the honest, devoted, self-controlled Romans, Christianity became a moral philosophy and a moral culture. Yet the text judges that it did not fully serve them as religion in the sense of an individual experience of spiritual growth.

head: Who
What they provided
rows: Unity of religious thought and practice

p195.s2.h: III–IV. Under the Roman Empire; The European Dark Ages — A Spark That Did Not Go Out
p195.s2.b0: The Christians had a God but no empire; the Greco-Romans had an empire but no God. So the Christians accepted the empire, and the empire adopted Christianity. To people whose language did not even have a word for unselfishness, this religion came as fresh comfort and liberation. The teaching that Christ loved little children brought an end to the practice of exposing unwanted infants, especially girls.
p195.s2.b2: But the new religion came too late to halt the moral decline of the empire. The text counts it a misfortune that it became a cultural necessity rather than a means of spiritual salvation. Because the church had allied itself with politics, it shared the decline of the Dark Ages, and the individual almost disappeared before the authority and tradition of the church. Still, Christianity endured that long night and survived to the dawn of the Renaissance.
p195.s2.b3: The text sums up this history as a single trajectory: beginning with the change from the religion of Jesus to a religion about Jesus, it passed through Hellenization and paganization, secularization and institutionalization, decline, stagnation, and hibernation, threatened extinction and rejuvenation, fragmentation, and finally a relative recovery. This tenacity shows its inherent vitality. And now Christianity faces an even more ominous struggle for survival in an age of scientific thinking and materialism.
p195.s3.h: V. The Modern Problem — What Religion Is and Is Not
p195.s3.b0: The more civilization advances, the more necessary it becomes to seek first the realities of heaven. Truth that is fragmented and overanalyzed easily misleads; it leads aright only when grasped as a whole, as a living spiritual reality. The text clearly distinguishes religion from other high forms of thought.

head: Form of thought distinct from religion
Its object
rows: The contrast of beauty and ugliness
The discovery of cosmic values that produces faith and assurance, culminating in worship

p195.s3.b3: This section also holds gentle counsel for modern people. Do not try to satisfy every urge for adventure within one short lifetime; be patient, for a career of endless discovery lies ahead. And when you see the evil in the world, remember that it is a black spot on a white background of goodness, and do not talk too much about evil when there is so much good truth to tell.
p195.s4.h: VI–VII. Materialism; The Vulnerability of Materialism — A Machine Does Not Know It Is a Machine
p195.s4.b0: Scientists have unintentionally thrown mankind into a materialistic panic. But the text says that the spiritual bank of humanity holds enormous reserves that can withstand the run, and that the religion of Jesus will be shown never to have been bankrupt. True religion cannot be at odds with science; what science has destroyed are only the childish illusions that misinterpreted life.

head: Science
Religion
rows: Deals with origins, values, and goals
Lives by the mathematics of the mind
The spirit rhythm of the soul in harmony with the melody of the infinite
Demonstrates the conservation of the human soul
Not science but the scientist perceives the universe
Not religion but the religionist demonstrates spirit reality

p195.s4.b2: The text’s argument against materialism is simple yet sharp. If the universe were purely a machine and man only a machine, man could not even know that he is a machine. The very concept of mechanism is a nonmaterial phenomenon of mind. A machine cannot know truth, hunger for righteousness, or cherish goodness.
p195.s4.b4: The text says that materialism, mechanism, and determinism exist, but they are not the whole story. Freedom and initiative are proportional to the degree to which one does the Father’s will. The sentence that follows is a great comfort to every reader who seeks God.
p195.s4.b6: One of the great problems of the modern age is the feeling of being too busy to find time for spiritual meditation and devotion. Another great error is that religious leaders try to call modern people with the trumpet blasts of the Middle Ages. Religion must equip itself with new slogans suited to its time.
p195.s5.h: VIII. Secular Totalitarianism — From the Church’s Fetters to the State’s
p195.s5.b0: The text identifies the father of modern secularism as godless science and its mother as the totalitarian medieval church. Secularism began as a protest against the domination of the church and broke its fetters, but now it hands people over to the political and economic slavery of the totalitarian state.
p195.s5.b1: Yet the text keeps its balance. It warns against hastily throwing away the blessings of the secular revolt — tolerance, social service, democratic government, and civil liberties. The great mistake of secularism was that, having rebelled against the church, it went on to rebel against God himself. There was no need to abandon faith in order to enjoy those blessings.
p195.s6.h: IX–X. Christianity’s Problem; The Future — Back to Jesus
p195.s6.b0: The text diagnoses Christianity soberly. Paganized and socialized Christianity needs new contact with the uncompromised teachings of Jesus. It is slowly dying of formalism, overorganization, intellectualism, and other nonspiritual trends. People take their religion secondhand, just as their teachers hand it down to them.
p195.s6.b2: Modern intellectuals shy away from the religion of Jesus because they fear it will dominate and transform them. The text says their fear is well founded, for the religion of Jesus really does ask people to devote their lives to knowing the Father’s will and to pour their energies into unselfish service of the brotherhood.
p195.s6.b4: The text says it is futile to talk of reviving primitive Christianity. We must go forward from where we are and show the world Jesus living again in the experience of spirit-born mortals. Christianity willingly goes the first mile, but too few go the second mile of free service that holds a brother in love. The true church, the brotherhood of Jesus, is invisible and spiritual, characterized by unity, not uniformity.
p195.s6.b5: That is no reason to despise Christianity. It is the product of the combined moral genius of many ages and peoples, and it has been one of the greatest powers for good on earth. The teachings set in motion by commonplace disciples conquered the Roman world in three hundred years, and after a thousand-year coma it resurrected itself.
p195.s7.b0: Paper 195 is a paper of criticism and of hope. Christianity won the world by compromise and dimmed Jesus’ ideals as the price. Yet those ideals still lie latent in the gospel, and an age of materialism and secularism is in fact a time ripe for great revelation. In the end, hope lies in learning anew the living gospel of the fatherhood of God and the brotherhood of man.

p195.s7.b3: The next paper, Paper 196, “The Faith of Jesus,” the last paper of the book, looks into the faith that Jesus himself held.
p196.lead: Not belief about Jesus but the faith Jesus himself held: The Urantia Book closes with that childlike but never childish faith and with the supremacy of religion.

p196.foot.text: Narrated by a secondary midwayer once assigned to the Apostle Andrew

p196.s0.h: Introduction — What the Last Paper Asks
p196.s0.b0: The last paper of The Urantia Book is concerned less with what Jesus did than with how he believed. Jesus enjoyed a sublime and wholehearted faith in God. He passed through all the ordinary ups and downs of mortal life, yet he never religiously doubted God’s watchcare. His faith was neither inherited from tradition nor an intellectual conclusion; it was a personal, spiritual insight born of the activity of the indwelling Adjuster.
p196.s0.b1: He saw God not only as holy, just, and great but also as true, beautiful, and good, and he unified all these attributes as “the will of the Father in heaven.” The idea of calling God Father did not originate with him, but he exalted it into a sublime experience and proclaimed every mortal a child of that Father.

head: What Jesus’ faith was not
What Jesus’ faith was
rows: A struggling soul clinging to faith at war with a hostile world
The thrill of living, in tranquillity, in the very presence of the Father
A consolation in difficulty or a comfort in despair
A living experience of actual spirit attainment
Reverence for tradition or intellectual belief in a creed
A sublime experience and a profound conviction that held him securely
A personal, original, and spontaneous spiritual faith

p196.s0.b3: The text says that Jesus’ great contribution was not that he revealed many new ideas about God, but that he so magnificently and humanly demonstrated a new and higher type of living faith in God.
p196.s1.h: Faith in Daily Life — Faith Without Fanaticism, a Life of Prayer
p196.s1.b0: Strong spiritual faith in religious geniuses often slides into fanaticism and exaggerated ego. But Jesus’ faith never overrode the judgments of practical life. He respected personal honor, family love, religious obligation, social duty, and economic necessity, and he harmonized them all with his faith. Even in his intense mission there was never the rage of a fanatic or the bluster of a religious egotist.
p196.s1.b1: He dedicated his own will to the service of doing the divine will and interpreted religion wholly in terms of the Father’s will. He never prayed as a religious duty. The secret of his unparalleled religious life was his consciousness of the presence of God, which he attained not by visions or extraordinary practices but by intelligent prayer and sincere worship.

head: To Jesus, prayer was
Among the expressions the text lists
rows: A sincere expression of spiritual attitude, a declaration of soul loyalty, a declaration of faith, a confession of supreme devotion
An avoidance of emotional tension, a prevention of conflict, a clarification of viewpoint
An exaltation of intellection, an ennoblement of desire, an enrichment of thought
A vindication of moral decision, a transcendental surrender of will, a revelation of courage
A technique for the adjustment of difficulties, the mobilization of the soul’s powers against selfishness, evil, and sin

p196.s1.b4: Jesus trusted God as a child trusts a parent, and believed in the fundamental goodness of the universe as a child believes in the security of home. Yet his faith was neither immature nor credulous. He joined a child’s trusting optimism with the intelligent courage of a mature adult, and his faith grew so high that it was without fear.
p196.s1.b7: Not only to believe what he believed but to believe as he believed: this is the full meaning of “Follow me.” The text adds that believing in this way takes a strong will and steadfast trust. Jesus’ faith was full of trust yet far from presumption, and it faced disappointment, difficulty, and the demands of duty with courage.
p196.s2.b0: However great the sovereignty of Michael, the human Jesus must not be taken away from men. He ascended on high as a man as well as God. The text says that debates about the humanity or divinity of Christ must not obscure the saving truth that he was a religious man who, by faith, knew and did the will of God.
p196.s2.b2: The text says the time has come for a figurative resurrection of the human Jesus from the burial tomb of nineteen centuries of theological tradition. To follow Jesus is not to imitate his outward life literally but to share his faith: to trust God as he trusted God, and to believe in people as he believed in people.
p196.s2.b4: As human beings advance from human consciousness to the realization of divinity, so Jesus ascended from human nature to the consciousness of divine nature. That ascent was the joint achievement of mortal faith and the work of the indwelling Adjuster, and it is marked by seven stages.

The messenger of Immanuel who appeared to him at Jerusalem when he was about twelve

p196.s3.h: II. The Religion of Jesus — Beyond a Religion About Jesus
p196.s3.b1: Here the thread traced through the last papers of Part IV is drawn together. Peter at Pentecost unintentionally inaugurated a new religion of the risen and glorified Christ, and Paul transformed it into Christianity, founded on his own experience. The text judges that the New Testament is a superb Christian document, but only meagerly portrays Jesus’ own religious life.

head: Point
The religion Jesus founded
The religion Paul founded
rows: The personal religious experience of the Jesus of Galilee
The experience of doing God’s will and serving the brotherhood
The glorified Jesus as the object of worship
All men as sons of God
Fellow believers in the divine Christ
The human Jesus had a religion
The divine Christ almost overnight became a religion

p196.s3.b3: The text calls it a great mistake to regard Jesus as wholly human or as only divine. He is still truly human and divine. And because his ascent from the human to the divine was wholly a mortal achievement, he became the new and living way by which every mortal may make the same ascent.
p196.s3.b4: Jesus led people to feel at home in the world. He taught that the world is not fundamentally evil, and he attained an ideal religious life in the very midst of the real world. He did not view humankind negatively; the high value he placed on people is why he poured himself out in ceaseless service.
p196.s4.h: III. The Supremacy of Religion — Fact, Meaning, and Value
p196.s4.b0: Personal, spiritual religious experience is an efficient solvent for most mortal difficulties. Religion does not remove problems, but it illuminates and transcends them. And it bridges the deep gulf between the intellectual logic that knows a First Cause of the universe and the soul’s affirmation that he is the Father in heaven of Jesus’ gospel.
p196.s4.b3: The human mind is not wholly material, for within it is a spirit nucleus, the Adjuster. The text gives three evidences of this spirit indwelling. The mind does not create values; it discovers, interprets, and chooses them, and moral values become ours through three choices: self-judgment, social judgment, and God-judgment.

head: Evidence of spirit indwelling
What it shows
rows: Only a spirit-indwelt intellect can love unselfishly and unconditionally
Only a spirit-indwelt mind can understand that the universe is friendly to the individual
Worship — the spiritual evaluation of life
Only a spirit-indwelt person can realize the divine presence and seek a fuller experience of it

p196.s4.b5: The text compares several religions to show Jesus’ place. The Hebrews achieved a religion of moral sublimity, the Greeks a religion of beauty, and Paul and his associates a religion of faith, hope, and charity. Jesus revealed and exemplified a religion of love: security in the Father’s love and the joy of sharing that love with one’s brothers. Yet love without truth, beauty, and goodness is only sentiment; love must be redefined on each level of progress.
p196.s4.b6: Religion stands above science, art, philosophy, and morals, yet it is not separate from them. God is not the invention of human idealism but the personality of love, the source of all that is true, beautiful, and good. And the great challenge to modern people is to achieve better communication with the divine Monitor who dwells within the mind.
p196.s5.h: Conclusion — Living This Paper, and This Book
p196.s5.b0: Paper 196 invites us to move from believing in Jesus to believing with Jesus. His faith trusted like a child yet was brave like an adult, burned warm without fanaticism, and was renewed daily in prayer and worship. And the paper’s last paragraph ends with a promise: the realities born of love and nurtured in service do not perish.
p196.s5.b1: That last sentence brings the whole book back to its beginning. In Paper 1, before anything else, The Urantia Book introduced the Universal Father. After the long journey through the central and superuniverses, the local universe, the history of Urantia, and the life and teachings of Jesus, the book returns to the Father and comes to rest.

rows: A Father who is a person we can know and love

p196.s5.b5: So the task left to the reader who has finished this book is not knowledge but life: not to stop at preaching a religion about Jesus, but to live the religion of Jesus — to trust God as Father and to serve all people as brothers and sisters. With this, the paper-by-paper commentary on The Urantia Book comes to its close.
